collection.description: On the morning tide, a little raft of lashed bamboo drifts into the lagoon.

ask.text:
On the morning tide, a little raft of lashed bamboo drifts into the lagoon. (Name) spots it first, and then spots the small shape clinging to it.
It's a child. Salt-crusted, sunburned and absolutely silent, gripping the bamboo so tightly that (name) has to pry (his/her) fingers loose one by one.
Tied to the raft's little pole are a gourd of water and a bundle wrapped carefully in leaves. The knots are neat and tight. Whoever sent this child off across the water did it with great care, and, (name) thinks with a lump in (his/her) throat, probably with great sorrow. The child needs looking after right away. But what should the village do about where the child came from?

choices.label: Wrap the Child in a Blanket
Let the Child Choose a Home

c1o1.text: The child is given a warm meal and a bed in the healer's hut, and sleeps for a full day and night without moving. When (he/she) finally wakes, the first thing (he/she) does is look for the raft. (Name) shows (him/her) it's safe on the beach, and the child relaxes, a little.

c1o2.text: The child sits up, unwraps the leaf bundle, and finds dried fish packed inside, by someone who loved (him/her). (He/She) looks at it for a long time. Then, shyly, without a word, (he/she) offers to share it with (name). The stores gain a little food, and (name) has to leave the hut for a minute.

c1.text: (Name) wraps the child in the first blanket (he/she) can find, and carries (him/her) straight up to the healers...

c2o1.text: Once the child can speak about it, (he/she) explains proudly how (his/her) family lashed the raft so it could never tip, with the bamboo crossed in a special pattern and tied double at every crossing. The builders are impressed, and learn something useful. The child seems pleased to have taught the grown-ups something.

c2o2.text: The child talks about many things, birds and shells and the colour of the sea, but won't talk about how (he/she) came to be on the raft. Whenever (name) gets close to it, (he/she) goes silent again. No one presses.

c2.text: Over the next few days, (name) sits with the child often, never pushing, just talking about small things. Slowly, the child begins to talk back...

c3o1.text: The child chooses to stay, and is welcomed into a household as a new villager, with more aunts and uncles than (he/she) can count. (He/She) keeps the raft's little pole by (his/her) sleeping mat. Some nights, (he/she) still looks out at the sea, but (he/she) always comes back in to the fire.

c3o2.text: Days later, a canoe arrives with the child's relatives, frantic, who have been searching every island for (him/her). The reunion on the beach makes everyone cry. The child goes home with them, waving until they are out of sight.

c3.text: After a week, the child has started following (name) everywhere, and the village begins to talk about what to do...

c4o1.text: The child helps pick breadfruit, and somewhere around the third tree, starts chattering for the first time: about the fruit, the birds, the size of the leaves. The harvest adds a good amount of food to the stores, but what everyone remembers is the sound of that small voice in the trees.

c4o2.text: While the villagers mend the battered raft, the child, calmer now, points out over the water: "Home is that way. Past the two rocks." Two fishers paddle (him/her) carefully back, and return to say the child's family wept with joy, and sent back a basket of shells in thanks.

c4.text: (Name) notices the child is happiest when (his/her) hands are busy. (He/She) starts giving (him/her) little jobs...
